summary:
Corrientes Province stands under Argentina's national framework, which remains among the most permissive in the world on legal gender recognition. Law 26.743 was approved by the Chamber of Deputies 167-17-7 and by the Senate on 9 May 2012 by 55 votes to one abstention, promulgated on 24 May 2012, and permits a change of legal gender without surgery, hormone treatment or judicial approval. The United Nations described it as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region. Argentina legalised marriage equality in 2010, the first Latin American country to do so, and anti-discrimination protection operates through a combination of national and provincial laws.

That framework has been narrowed by executive action that binds every province, Corrientes included. Emergency Decree 62/2025, issued on 5 February 2025, amends the Gender Identity Law to bar people under 18 from gender-affirming surgery and comprehensive hormonal treatment. Decree 61/2025 governs the placement of transgender people in the prison system. Reuters reported the surgery and hormone ban; legal experts interviewed by Agencia Presentes called both decrees unlawful and unconstitutional, and the Federación Argentina de Lesbianas, Gays, Bisexuales y Trans announced legal action seeking judicial intervention.

Two further national measures bear on a visitor's expectations. The government dismissed transgender people hired under the 1% public-sector Trans Labor Quota, and abolished INADI, the federal anti-discrimination agency that had received complaints.

Violence against LGBTIQ+ people reached a documented peak in 2025. The Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity over the year, a record, averaging one every 38 hours, with trans women bearing a disproportionate share of the harm. Activists interviewed in Buenos Aires in April 2025, including representatives of organisations named for Diana Sacayán, killed in 2015, and for the activist Lohana Berkins, said the national government's policies had made the community more vulnerable to violence and described the situation as chaotic and desperate.

Police violence against trans and travesti sex workers, already common, has worsened since the current national administration took office and is reported as worst outside Buenos Aires. A Washington Blade report of 10 April 2025 names Corrientes among the more conservative interior provinces where the situation is worse. No Corrientes-specific incident, arrest or prosecution record is sourced here.

The judicial response to gender-motivated killing is contested. In April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence imposed on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán while rejecting attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance that an appeals court removed in 2020, so that aggravation is not currently applied in that line of cases. Outright International's country overview, updated in March 2026, records negative assessments for same-sex relations, gender recognition and the registration of civil-society organisations, an assessment of deterioration against the earlier statutory position.
tangentialFactors:
The February 2025 decrees are national in reach, so the restrictions they impose on minors and on prison placement apply identically in Corrientes and in Buenos Aires City; the province offers no separate statutory position on either question.

Activists place the deterioration in a national pattern rather than a local one: police violence against trans and travesti sex workers is described as worst across the more conservative interior provinces, of which Corrientes is one example, and the 227 recorded hate crimes of 2025 are a nationwide figure.

The abolition of INADI removed the federal complaint channel that had handled discrimination reports, leaving provincial and judicial routes; how Corrientes substitutes for that channel is not sourced in this inventory.
localsOnly:
Residents of Corrientes, including trans and travesti people living there, are subject to Decree 62/2025, which bars under-18s from gender-affirming surgery and comprehensive hormonal treatment, and to Decree 61/2025 on the placement of transgender people in the prison system. Both decrees modify Law 26.743 as it applies within the province.

Transgender people employed in the national public sector under the 1% Trans Labor Quota were dismissed, and INADI, the federal anti-discrimination agency, was abolished, removing a route residents had used to report discrimination.

Sex workers who are trans or travesti face police violence that activists describe as common and worsening, with Corrientes named among the provinces where it is worse. The travesticidio aggravating circumstance in homicide cases was removed on appeal in the Sacayán case and was not reinstated by the Supreme Court in April 2025.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Corrientes-specific incident data, arrest records, prosecution outcomes or provincial anti-discrimination legislation are sourced in this inventory; the province's position rests on the national framework plus one April 2025 report naming it as an example of a wider interior pattern.

The outcome of the legal action announced by the Federación Argentina de Lesbianas, Gays, Bisexuales y Trans against Decrees 61/2025 and 62/2025 is unresolved in these sources, as is whether any court has since ruled the decrees unlawful.

How discrimination complaints are handled in Corrientes following INADI's abolition is not sourced. The Outright International assessment of March 2026 is a country-level rating and does not distinguish the province.
